implementation_notes: Scala decorates by mixing stackable traits into a core implementation: a trait that extends the component declares `abstract override def op(...) = { ...; super.op(...) }`, the abstract override tells the compiler the trait must be mixed after a concrete implementation, and the linearisation runs the rightmost trait first - so `new BasicQueue with Filtering with Doubling` stacks both modifications. Artima's formulation is precise about the difference: this is decoration for class composition rather than object composition, the same feature-composition arithmetic (N traits instead of 2^N subclasses) applied at compile time. Keep the classic GoF wrapper class - a Decorator holding a Component and forwarding - when the composition must be chosen per object instance at runtime, which is the one thing the trait form cannot express.
idiom_name: stackable traits with `abstract override` and `super` (mixin order = decoration order)
pitfalls: Order dependence is the semantics: the rightmost mixin executes first, so the same traits mixed in a different order produce different results and nothing at the call site records which order is intended.

abstract override is legal only in a trait and only works when a concrete implementation appears later in the linearisation; mixing such a trait without a core implementation compiles but fails when the super call is reached.

Trait stacking decorates a whole class, not an instance: two queues with different behaviour require two classes, and state added by a stackable trait is per-instance but shared by every instance of that mixin combination.
